claim: Reward-rate maximization is a prominent normative principle in behavioral ecology, neuroscience, economics, and AI.
source_text: Reward-rate maximization is a prominent normative principle in behavioral ecology, neuroscience, economics, and AI.
evidence_reasoning: This statement draws from established scientific consensus across multiple fields regarding reward-rate maximization as a normative principle.

claim: Time's cost consists of both apportionment and opportunity cost.
source_text: we show that time's cost consists of both apportionment and opportunity cost
evidence_reasoning: This claim is derived from mathematical analysis presented in the manuscript, supported by equations and logical inference from the reward-rate maximization framework.

claim: A reward-rate-optimal agent's discounting function combines hyperbolic and linear components reflecting apportionment and opportunity costs.
source_text: we show precisely how a reward-rate-optimal agent's discounting function (1) combines hyperbolic and linear components reflecting apportionment and opportunity costs
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through mathematical derivations and analysis of the discounting function presented in the manuscript.

claim: A reward-rate-optimal agent's discounting function is dependent not only on the considered pursuit's properties but also on time spent and rewards obtained outside the pursuit.
source_text: is dependent not only on the considered pursuit's properties but also on time spent and rewards obtained outside the pursuit
evidence_reasoning: This is shown through mathematical analysis demonstrating how outside time and reward parameters affect the discounting function.

claim: Hyperbolic discounting is consistent with reward-rate maximization.
source_text: This analysis reveals how purported signs of suboptimal behavior (hyperbolic discounting, and the Delay, Magnitude, and Sign effects) are in fact consistent with reward-rate maximization.
evidence_reasoning: The manuscript demonstrates through mathematical derivation that hyperbolic discounting emerges from reward-rate maximization principles.

claim: The Delay, Magnitude, and Sign effects are consistent with reward-rate maximization.
source_text: This analysis reveals how purported signs of suboptimal behavior (hyperbolic discounting, and the Delay, Magnitude, and Sign effects) are in fact consistent with reward-rate maximization.
evidence_reasoning: The manuscript provides mathematical analysis showing these effects arise naturally from reward-rate optimization.

claim: Suboptimal decisions likely stem from errors in assessing time's apportionment—specifically, underweighting time spent outside versus inside a pursuit.
source_text: we then analyze the impact of misestimating reward-rate-maximizing parameters and find that suboptimal decisions likely stem from errors in assessing time's apportionment—specifically, underweighting time spent outside versus inside a pursuit
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is based on systematic analysis of parameter misestimation effects presented in the manuscript.

claim: Animals seek to maximize reward rate while foraging in an environment according to Optimal Foraging Theory.
source_text: A normative principle with broad appeal identified in behavioral ecology is that of reward-rate maximization, as expressed in Optimal Foraging Theory (OFT), where animals seek to maximize reward rate while foraging in an environment
evidence_reasoning: This statement references established theory in behavioral ecology, supported by citations to Charnov, Krebs, and Pyke.

claim: Decisions about what pursuits should be taken are made on the basis of their subjective value.
source_text: It is widely assumed that decisions about what pursuits should be taken are made on the basis of their subjective value
evidence_reasoning: This reflects established assumptions in the field, supported by citation to Niv, 2009.

claim: Forgo decisions are regarded as near-optimal in prey selection.
source_text: Although 'Forgo' decisions are regarded as near-optimal, as in prey selection
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to behavioral ecology literature on prey selection.

claim: Choice decisions reveal a suboptimal bias for smaller-sooner rewards when selection of later-larger rewards would maximize the reward rate.
source_text: 'Choice' decisions—as commonly tested in laboratory settings—reveal a suboptimal bias for smaller-sooner (SS) rewards when selection of later-larger rewards would maximize the reward rate while foraging in an environment
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies showing this behavioral pattern.

claim: Steeper temporal discounting has been associated with many negative life outcomes.
source_text: An understanding of the form of temporal discounting has important implications in life, as steeper temporal discounting has been associated with many negative life outcomes
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by multiple citations to studies linking temporal discounting to negative outcomes.

claim: Steeper temporal discounting is associated with the risk of developing an addiction.
source_text: steeper temporal discounting has been associated with many negative life outcomes (Bretteville-Jensen, 1999; Critchfield and Kollins, 2001; Bickel et al., 2007; Bickel et al., 2012; Story et al., 2014), most notably the risk of developing an addiction
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to studies on addiction and temporal discounting.

claim: Animals' temporal discounting in intertemporal choice tasks is well-fit by a hyperbolic discounting function.
source_text: Psychologists and behavioral scientists have long found that animals' temporal discounting in intertemporal choice tasks is well-fit by a hyperbolic discounting function
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies showing hyperbolic fits to animal behavior.

claim: Exponential discounting was derived from the normative principle of time consistency.
source_text: An exponential discounting function, for instance, was derived by Samuelson from the normative principle of time consistency
evidence_reasoning: This references Samuelson's theoretical work on exponential discounting.

claim: Exponential discounting is widely held as rational.
source_text: An exponential discounting function, for instance, was derived by Samuelson from the normative principle of time consistency (Samuelson, 1937) and is widely held as rational
evidence_reasoning: This reflects consensus in economics literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Observed temporal decision-making behavior routinely exhibits time inconsistencies.
source_text: Observed temporal decision-making behavior, however, routinely exhibits time inconsistencies
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to empirical studies documenting time inconsistencies.

claim: Observed temporal decision-making behavior is better fit by a hyperbolic discounting function than exponential.
source_text: Observed temporal decision-making behavior, however, routinely exhibits time inconsistencies (Strotz, 1955; Ainslie, 1975; Laibson, 1997; Frederick et al., 2002) and is better fit by a hyperbolic discounting function
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to empirical studies comparing model fits.

claim: Humans and animals have commonly been regarded as irrational based on hyperbolic discounting.
source_text: on that contrasting basis, humans and animals have commonly been regarded as irrational
evidence_reasoning: This reflects a common interpretation in the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Magnitude Effect refers to the observation that the apparent discounting function is affected by the magnitude of the offered pursuit's outcome.
source_text: the case that humans and animals are irrational is, ostensibly, furthered by the observation of the 'Magnitude Effect' (Benzion et al., 1989; Green et al., 1994; Green et al., 1997; Frederick et al., 2002; Baker et al., 2003; Estle et al., 2006; Yi et al., 2006; Grace et al., 2012; Kinloch and White, 2013)
evidence_reasoning: This defines the Magnitude Effect based on cited empirical observations.

claim: The Sign Effect refers to the observation that the apparent discounting function is affected by the sign of the offered pursuit's outcome.
source_text: the 'Sign Effect' (Thaler and Shefrin, 1981b; Loewenstein and Thaler, 1989; Loewenstein and Prelec, 1992; Frederick et al., 2002; Baker et al., 2003; Estle et al., 2006; Kalenscher and Pennartz, 2008) where the apparent discounting function is affected by the magnitude and the sign of the offered pursuit's outcome, respectively
evidence_reasoning: This defines the Sign Effect based on cited empirical observations.

claim: The Delay Effect refers to preference between pursuits switching as the time required for their obtainment changes.
source_text: the 'Delay Effect', where preference between pursuits can switch as the time required for their obtainment changes
evidence_reasoning: This defines the Delay Effect based on cited empirical observations.

claim: A temporal decision-making world is composed of pursuits.
source_text: A temporal decision-making world is one composed of pursuits.
evidence_reasoning: This is a definitional framework established by the authors for their analysis.

claim: A pursuit has a reward magnitude and a time.
source_text: Pursuits have a reward magnitude (r) and a time (t).
evidence_reasoning: This is a definitional component of the authors' framework.

claim: A pursuit has a reward rate and a weight.
source_text: A pursuit therefore has (1) a reward rate (⍴, rho) and (2) a weight (w), being its relative occupancy with respect to all other pursuits.
evidence_reasoning: This follows logically from the definitions of reward magnitude and time.

claim: The global reward rate is the reward rate achieved under a reward-rate maximal policy.
source_text: the global reward rate achieved under a reward-rate maximal policy will be denoted as ρg∗
evidence_reasoning: This is a definitional statement within the authors' framework.

claim: There are two fundamental types of decisions regarding whether to initiate a pursuit: Forgo decisions and Choice decisions.
source_text: we now identify two fundamental types of decisions regarding whether to initiate a pursuit: 'Forgo' decisions, and 'Choice' decisions.
evidence_reasoning: This is a categorization established by the authors for their analysis.

claim: In a Forgo decision, the agent is presented with one pursuit that can either be accepted or rejected.
source_text: In a Forgo decision (Figure 1, left), the agent is presented with one of possibly many pursuits (and see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2) that can either be accepted or rejected.
evidence_reasoning: This is a definitional description of the Forgo decision scenario.

claim: In a Choice decision, the agent is presented with a choice between at least two simultaneous and mutually exclusive pursuits.
source_text: In a Choice decision (Figure 1, right), the agent is presented with a choice between at least two simultaneous and mutually exclusive pursuits, typically differing in their respective rewards' magnitudes and delays.
evidence_reasoning: This is a definitional description of the Choice decision scenario.

claim: Animals are optimal or virtually optimal in Forgo decisions.
source_text: Experimental observation in temporal decision-making demonstrates that animals are optimal (or virtually so) in Forgo
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on prey selection and foraging behavior.

claim: Animals are suboptimally impatient in Choice decisions, selecting the SS pursuit when the LL pursuit is reward-rate-maximizing.
source_text: are as if sub-optimally impatient in Choice, selecting the SS pursuit when the LL pursuit is reward-rate-maximizing
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on intertemporal choice.

claim: The global reward rate of an environment can be calculated using Equation 1.
source_text: it becomes possible to calculate the total global reward rate of the environment, ρg, as in Equation 1
evidence_reasoning: This is derived mathematically in the manuscript and presented in Appendix 1.

claim: The environment may be parcellated into the time spent and rewards achieved inside the considered pursuit and everything else outside the considered pursuit.
source_text: The environment may be parcellated into the time spent and rewards achieved inside the considered pursuit on average, for every instance that time is spent and rewards achieved outside the considered pursuit, on average.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conceptual framework developed through mathematical reformulation in the manuscript.

claim: The global reward rate is a weighted average of the local reward rates of the pursuits constituting the world.
source_text: Therefore, the global reward rate is the sum of the local reward rates of the world's constituent pursuits under a given policy when weighted by their relative occupancy: the weighted average of the local reward rates of the pursuits constituting the world
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through mathematical derivation in Equation 6 and Appendix 4.

claim: Global reward rate can be maximized by iteratively forgoing the considered pursuit if its reward rate is less than its outside reward rate.
source_text: Global reward rate can be maximized by iteratively forgoing the considered pursuit if its reward rate is less than its outside reward rate, ρin<ρout
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from the mathematical analysis of optimal policies in Appendix 5.

claim: The subjective value of a pursuit is the amount of immediate reward requiring no time investment that yields the same global reward rate as that arising from a policy of taking the pursuit.
source_text: the amount of immediate reward that would be accepted in place of its initiation and attainment could serve as a metric of the pursuit's worth at the time of its initiation
evidence_reasoning: This is a conceptual definition developed and formalized in Equation 7.

claim: The subjective value of a pursuit corresponds to the subtraction of the cost of time from the pursuit's reward.
source_text: Therefore, the equivalent immediate reward of a pursuit, its subjective value, corresponds to the subtraction of the cost of time from the pursuit's reward.
evidence_reasoning: This is shown through mathematical derivation in Equation 7.

claim: The cost of time of a considered pursuit is the global reward rate of the world under a policy of accepting the pursuit, times the time that the pursuit would take.
source_text: The cost of time of a considered pursuit is the global reward rate of the world under a policy of accepting the pursuit, times the time that the pursuit would take, ρgtin
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from the mathematical analysis and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Time's cost comprises an apportionment cost as well as an opportunity cost.
source_text: Expressing subjective value in terms of the outside reward rate and time reveals that a portion of a pursuit's time cost arises from an opportunity cost
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through mathematical reformulation in Equation 8 and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The opportunity cost associated with a considered pursuit is the reward rate outside the considered pursuit type times the time of the considered pursuit.
source_text: The opportunity cost associated with a considered pursuit, ρouttin, is the reward rate outside the considered pursuit type, ρout, times the time of the considered pursuit, tin
evidence_reasoning: This is defined and illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: Apportionment cost is the difference in reward that can be expected between a policy of taking versus not taking the considered pursuit, over a time equal to its duration.
source_text: From the perspective of decision-making policies, apportionment cost is the difference in reward that can be expected, on average, between a policy of taking versus a policy of not taking the considered pursuit, over a time equal to its duration
evidence_reasoning: This is derived and formalized in Equation 9.

claim: The subjective value of a pursuit decreases linearly as the outside reward increases when outside time is held constant.
source_text: Plotting the subjective value of the pursuit (green dots in B) as a function of increasing the outside reward (green dotted line in C through F) reveals that the subjective value of the pursuit decreases linearly.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through analysis and illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: As outside reward increases, the opportunity cost of time increases linearly.
source_text: As the outside reward increases, the opportunity cost of time increases linearly.
evidence_reasoning: This is shown through analysis and illustrated in Figure 6D.

claim: As outside reward increases, the apportionment cost of time decreases linearly.
source_text: As the outside reward increases, the apportionment cost of time decreases linearly, becomes zero when the inside and outside reward rates are equal, and then becomes negative
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through analysis and illustrated in Figure 6E.

claim: When outside reward rate is zero, time's cost is composed entirely of apportionment cost.
source_text: When the outside reward is zero, there is zero opportunity cost of time (Figure 6D and F orange dots), with time's cost being entirely constituted by the apportionment cost of time
evidence_reasoning: This is shown through analysis and illustrated in Figure 6F.

claim: The subjective value of a pursuit increases hyperbolically as outside time increases when outside reward is held constant at zero.
source_text: When apportionment cost (brown annuli) solely composes the cost of time, the cost of time decreases hyperbolically as the outside time increases, resulting in the subjective value of a pursuit increasing hyperbolically
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through analysis and illustrated in Figure 7D.

claim: The subjective value of a pursuit increases hyperbolically as outside time increases when outside reward is held constant at a non-zero value.
source_text: Plotting the subjective value-by-outside time function (green dotted line) then reveals that subjective value increases hyperbolically under these conditions as outside time increases
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through analysis and illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: A reward-rate-optimal agent will appear more patient the longer the time spent outside a considered pursuit.
source_text: A reward-rate-optimal agent will thus appear as if more patient (1) the longer the time spent outside a considered pursuit
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from the analysis of how outside time affects subjective value.

claim: A reward-rate-optimal agent will appear more patient the lower the outside reward rate.
source_text: A reward-rate-optimal agent will thus appear as if more patient (1) the longer the time spent outside a considered pursuit, (2) the lower the outside reward rate
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from the analysis of how outside reward rate affects subjective value.

claim: The temporal discounting function of a reward-rate-optimal agent is a hyperbolic function.
source_text: Doing so illustrates how the mathematical form of the temporal discount function—as it appears for the optimal agent—is a hyperbolic function.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through mathematical derivation in Equation 11 and illustrated in Figure 13.

claim: The temporal discounting function's form depends wholly on the temporal reward structure of the environment.
source_text: This function's form depends wholly on the temporal reward structure of the environment and is composed of hyperbolic and linear components which relate to the apportionment and to the opportunity cost of time.
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from the mathematical analysis of the discounting function.

claim: In worlds in which no net reward is received outside a considered pursuit, the apparent discounting function is purely hyperbolic.
source_text: First, in worlds in which no net reward is received outside a considered pursuit, the apparent discounting function is purely hyperbolic
evidence_reasoning: This is shown through mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 13A.

claim: The curvature of the hyperbolic component is controlled by how much time the agent spends in versus outside the considered pursuit.
source_text: The curvature of the hyperbolic component is thus controlled by how much time the agent spends 'in' versus 'outside' the considered pursuit
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 13B.

claim: The more time spent outside the pursuit, the gentler the curvature of apparent hyperbolic discounting and the more patient the agent appears.
source_text: with the more time spent outside the pursuit, the gentler the curvature of apparent hyperbolic discounting and the more patient the agent appears to become for the considered pursuit
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from the mathematical analysis of the discounting function.

claim: The apparent discounting function will become steeper the more outside reward is obtained.
source_text: Third, in worlds in which reward is received outside a considered pursuit (compare B to C), the apparent discounting function will become steeper the more outside reward is obtained, as the linear component relating the opportunity cost of time increases.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through analysis and illustrated in Figure 13C.

claim: The Delay Effect (preference reversal) is not a sign of suboptimal decision making.
source_text: preference reversal, despite the magnitudes and the time between the options remaining unchanged, is taken as a sign of anomalous decision making (Cruz Rambaud et al., 2023). Figure 14 illustrates why preference reversal under increasing delay is not a sign of suboptimal decision-making but rather is consistent with reward-rate maximization.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through analysis showing that preference reversal emerges from reward-rate maximization, illustrated in Figure 14.

claim: A reward-rate-maximizing agent would exhibit the Magnitude Effect.
source_text: Therefore, the 'Magnitude Effect', as observed in humans and animals, would also be exhibited by a reward-rate-maximizing agent.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through analysis showing how the Magnitude Effect emerges from reward-rate maximization, illustrated in Figure 15.

claim: A reward-rate-maximizing agent would exhibit the Sign Effect.
source_text: We postulate that the value learning algorithm and representational architecture selected for by evolution has favored the ability to appreciate the reward rates of pursuits over that of their weights.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through analysis showing how the Sign Effect emerges from reward-rate maximization, illustrated in Figure 16.

claim: Forgo decision-making is observed to be near optimal in controlled experimental situations.
source_text: In controlled experimental situations, forgo decision-making is observed to be near optimal, consistent with observations from the field of behavioral ecology
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on foraging behavior.

claim: A suboptimal bias for SS rewards is widely reported in Choice decision-making in situations where selection of later-larger rewards would maximize global reward rate.
source_text: In contrast, a suboptimal bias for SS rewards is widely reported in Choice decision-making in situations where selection of later-larger rewards would maximize global reward rate
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on intertemporal choice.

claim: Humans and animals act as if sub-optimally impatient under Choice, while exhibiting near-optimal decision-making under Forgo decisions.
source_text: Collectively, the pattern of temporal decision-making behavior observed under Forgo and Choice decisions shows that humans and animals act as if sub-optimally impatience under Choice, while exhibiting near-optimal decision-making under Forgo decisions.
evidence_reasoning: This summarizes the pattern of experimental observations cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Only errors in time apportionment that underweight the outside time will accord with experimentally observed temporal decision-making regarding whether to initiate a pursuit.
source_text: Only errors in time apportionment that underweight the outside time, (or, equivalently, overweight the inside time)―while maintaining the true inside and outside reward rates―will accord with experimentally observed temporal decision-making regarding whether to initiate a pursuit.
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from systematic analysis of parameter misestimation effects presented in Figure 18.

claim: Underestimation of the relative time spent outside versus inside a considered pursuit is the likely source of error committed by animals and humans in temporal decision-making.
source_text: we implicate underestimation of the relative time spent outside versus in the considered pursuit type as the likely source of error committed by animals and humans in temporal decision-making that underlies their suboptimal pursuit valuation
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is based on analysis of parameter misestimation effects and comparison to observed behavior.

claim: Previous experimental observations are consistent with an agent underestimating the time spent outside the considered pursuit.
source_text: Previous experimental observations are consistent with, and have been interpreted as an agent underestimating the time spent outside the considered pursuit
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to experimental studies showing this pattern.

claim: Underestimation of post-reward delays is consistent with underestimating the time spent outside the considered pursuit.
source_text: as would occur with underestimation of post-reward delays
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to studies on post-reward delay estimation and logical inference.

claim: When a temporal decision world can be bisected into two components, only the reward rates need be accurately appreciated for the agent to optimally perform forgo decisions.
source_text: Thus, when a temporal decision world can effectively be bisected into two components, as often the case in experimental situations, only the reward rates, but not the weights of those portions need be accurately appreciated for the agent to optimally perform forgo decisions.
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from the mathematical analysis of optimal forgo policies.

claim: Misestimation of the weights of pursuits comprising a world would result in errors in valuation regarding the initiation of a pursuit under choice instances.
source_text: Misestimation of the weights of pursuits comprising a world would then result in errors in valuation regarding the initiation of a pursuit under choice instances.
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from the analysis of how weight misestimation affects choice decisions.

claim: The Malapportionment Hypothesis identifies the underweighting of the time spent outside versus inside a considered pursuit as the source of error committed by animals and humans.
source_text: We term this reckoning of the source of error committed by animals and humans the Malapportionment Hypothesis, which identifies the underweighting of the time spent outside versus inside a considered pursuit but not the misestimation of pursuit rates, as the source of error committed by animals and humans
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' proposed hypothesis based on their analysis of parameter misestimation effects.

claim: The Malapportionment Hypothesis captures previously published behavioral observations showing that animals can make optimal forgo decisions but suboptimal choice decisions.
source_text: This hypothesis therefore captures previously published behavioral observations (Figure 21A) showing that animals can make decisions to take or forgo reward options that optimize reward accumulation (Krebs et al., 1977; Stephens and Krebs, 1987; Blanchard and Hayden, 2014), but make suboptimal decisions when presented with simultaneous and mutually exclusive choices between rewards of different delays
evidence_reasoning: This connects the proposed hypothesis to existing experimental observations through citations and analysis.

claim: The Malapportionment Hypothesis predicts that apparent discounting functions will present with greater curvature than what a reward-rate-maximizing agent would exhibit.
source_text: The Malapportionment Hypothesis further predicts that apparent discounting functions will present with greater curvature than what a reward-rate-maximizing agent would exhibit
evidence_reasoning: This is a prediction derived from the Malapportionment Hypothesis and illustrated in Figure 21B.

claim: The Malapportionment Hypothesis predicts that the Magnitude and Sign Effect would be less pronounced than what a reward-rate-maximizing agent would exhibit.
source_text: the Malapportionment Hypothesis also predicts that the Magnitude (Figure 21C) and Sign Effect (Figure 21D) would be less pronounced than what a reward-rate-maximizing agent would exhibit
evidence_reasoning: This is a prediction derived from the Malapportionment Hypothesis and illustrated in Figures 21C and 21D.

claim: The Malapportionment Hypothesis predicts that preference reversal would occur at delays greater than that exhibited by a reward-rate-maximizing agent.
source_text: with regards to the Delay Effect (Figure 21E), the Malapportionment Hypothesis predicts that preference reversal would occur at delays greater than that exhibited by a reward-rate-maximizing agent
evidence_reasoning: This is a prediction derived from the Malapportionment Hypothesis and illustrated in Figure 21E.

claim: Hyperbolic functions are better fits to choice behavior in intertemporal choice tasks than exponential functions.
source_text: experimental observations have demonstrated that hyperbolic functions are better fits to choice behavior in intertemporal choice tasks than exponential functions
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to empirical studies comparing model fits.

claim: In most intertemporal choice tasks, animal behavior is far from optimal for maximizing reward rate.
source_text: Nonetheless, and problematically for OFT, in most intertemporal choice tasks, animal behavior is far from optimal for maximizing reward rate
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on intertemporal choice.

claim: Animals and humans typically exhibit much too great a preference for SS rewards in apparent discounting of delayed rewards with respect to global reward-rate maximization.
source_text: Indeed, with respect to global reward-rate maximization, animals and humans typically exhibit much too great a preference for SS rewards in apparent discounting of delayed rewards
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by extensive citations to experimental studies on temporal discounting.

claim: Mazur introduced 1+k into the denominator of the hyperbolic discounting function to address issues with Ainslie's original formulation.
source_text: Mazur, 1987 addressed these issues by introducing 1+k into the denominator, providing for the now standard hyperbolic discounting function
evidence_reasoning: This references Mazur's theoretical contribution to the hyperbolic discounting model.

claim: The free-fit parameter k has become widely interpreted as a psychological trait, such as patience, or willingness to delay gratification.
source_text: Introduction of the free-fit parameter, k, accommodated the variability observed across and within subjects by controlling the curvature of temporal discounting, and has become widely interpreted as a psychological trait, such as patience, or willingness to delay gratification
evidence_reasoning: This reflects common interpretation in the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Discounting functions have been directly incorporated into numerous models.
source_text: Indeed, discounting functions have been directly incorporated into numerous models
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to various models incorporating discounting functions.

claim: Best fits of discounting functions differ in steepness when the time spent outside the pursuit changes.
source_text: discounting function formulations must also contend with the fact that best fits differ in steepness (1) when the time spent and (2) reward gained outside the pursuit changes
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to experimental studies showing this effect.

claim: Best fits of discounting functions differ in steepness when the reward gained outside the pursuit changes.
source_text: discounting function formulations must also contend with the fact that best fits differ in steepness (1) when the time spent and (2) reward gained outside the pursuit changes
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to experimental studies showing this effect.

claim: Experiments with shorter intertrial intervals exhibit steeper apparent temporal discounting.
source_text: Indeed, experiments with shorter intertrial intervals, and thus higher global reward rates, have a higher cost of time, and therefore exhibit steeper apparent temporal discounting
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to experimental studies showing this relationship.

claim: Typical hyperbolic discounting models fail to account for the opportunity cost of time.
source_text: underscoring, how typical hyperbolic discounting models fail to account for the opportunity cost of time
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from comparison of the standard hyperbolic model to the reward-rate-optimal formulation.

claim: The failure to account for the opportunity cost of time would lead to aberrantly high values of k.
source_text: Should k be understood as representing time's apportionment cost, the failure to account for the opportunity cost of time would lead to aberrantly high values of k.
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from analysis of how the standard hyperbolic model compensates for missing the opportunity cost term.

claim: Standard hyperbolic discounting functions lack an accounting of the opportunity cost.
source_text: As typical hyperbolic discounting functions are of the form...DiscountFunction=11+kt...they lack an accounting of the opportunity cost
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from comparison of the standard form to the reward-rate-optimal formulation.

claim: Discounting models of the standard hyperbolic form are only appropriate in worlds with no outside reward.
source_text: Discounting models of the standard hyperbolic form are therefore only appropriate in worlds with no 'outside' reward, as under such conditions opportunity cost is zero.
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from analysis of when the standard hyperbolic form matches the reward-rate-optimal formulation.

claim: Many investigations into temporal discounting often do not make an explicit distinction between situations where subjects continue to receive rewards during delay versus situations where no other rewards occur during delay.
source_text: we also note that many investigations into temporal discounting often do not make an explicit distinction between situations in which (1) subjects continue to receive the usual rewards from the environment during the delay to a chosen pursuit and (2) situations in which during a chosen pursuit's delay no other rewards or opportunities will occur
evidence_reasoning: This is an observation about experimental design practices, supported by citations.

claim: Human subjects are commonly asked to answer questions about preferences for amounts they will not actually earn after delays they will not actually have to wait.
source_text: Commonly, human subjects are asked to answer questions about their preferences between options for amounts they will not actually earn after delays they will not actually have to wait
evidence_reasoning: This describes common experimental practices in human studies, supported by citation.

claim: In most animal experiments, subjects actually receive reward after different delays during which they do not receive new options or rewards.
source_text: In contrast, in most animal experiments, subjects actually receive reward after different delays during which they do not receive new options or rewards.
evidence_reasoning: This describes common experimental practices in animal studies.

claim: When being engaged in a pursuit does not exclude the agent from receiving rewards at the outside rate, the opportunity cost of time drops out of the subjective value equation.
source_text: By our formulation, when being engaged in a pursuit does not exclude the agent from receiving rewards at the rate that occurs outside, the opportunity cost of time drops out of the subjective value equation
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from the mathematical formulation and presented in Equation 12 and Appendix 12.

claim: Human discounting functions are often reported to be less steep than animal discounting functions because humans are typically tested in conditions that negate opportunity cost.
source_text: This rationalizes why human discounting functions are often reported to be less steep than animal discounting functions: they are typically tested in conditions that negate opportunity cost, whereas animals are typically tested in conditions that enforce opportunity costs.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference based on the analysis of opportunity cost and knowledge of experimental practices.

claim: When humans are made to wait for actually received reward, their observed discounting functions are much steeper.
source_text: Indeed, when humans are made to wait for actually received reward, their observed discounting functions are much steeper
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to an empirical study by Jimura et al., 2009.

claim: The standard hyperbolic discounting function cannot fit negative subjective values.
source_text: The standard hyperbolic discounting function, lacking accounting of opportunity cost, cannot fit negative subjective values and therefore would not predict when―or even that―an agent will forgo a rewarding pursuit.
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from analysis of the mathematical properties of the standard hyperbolic function.

claim: The Magnitude Effect should diminish when increasing the outside time while holding the outside reward constant.
source_text: The Magnitude Effect should be observed, experimentally, to diminish when (1) increasing the outside time while holding the outside reward constant, (thus decreasing the outside reward rate)
evidence_reasoning: This is a prediction derived from the reward-rate-optimal framework.

claim: Patience oughtn't imply a willingness to wait a longer time.

evidence_reasoning: This is a conceptual clarification derived from the reward-rate-optimal framework.

claim: The amount of time a reward-rate-maximizing agent is willing to invest isn't an intrinsic property of the agent itself but a consequence of the temporal decision-making world's reward-time structure.

claim: A reward-rate-optimal agent doesn't become more or less patient as the context changes; rather, it is precisely patient, under all circumstances.
source_text: So, if patience is to mean investing the 'correct' amount of time (i.e. the reward-rate-maximizing time), then a reward-rate-optimal agent doesn't become more or less patient as the context of what is otherwise the same pursuit changes; rather, it is precisely patient, under all circumstances.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conceptual clarification derived from the definition of optimal behavior.

claim: The essential feature of the TIMERR model is that the agent looks back into its near past to estimate the reward rate of the environment.

claim: TIMERR commits an overestimation of the outside reward rate, and thus, an overestimation of global reward rate, manifesting as suboptimal impatience in Choice and Forgo decisions.

claim: TIMERR is not in accordance with the Malapportionment Hypothesis as it mistakes pursuits' rates as well as their weights.
source_text: In this way, while TIMERR is appealing in assuming that the recent past is used to estimate the global reward rate, and reproduces a number of sensitivities to conditions observed behaviorally, it is not in accordance with the Malapportionment Hypothesis as it mistakes pursuits' rates as well as their weights―something is still amiss.
evidence_reasoning: This is a critical assessment comparing the TIMERR model to the Malapportionment Hypothesis.
